title: Explain the classic quadratic bottom-up tabulation for the Longest Increasing Subsequence, how each cell is built from earlier cells, how to reconstruct the actual subsequence with predecessor pointers, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: LIS Tabulation (Quadratic Bottom-Up and Reconstructing the Sequence)
keyPoints: Each cell len[i] holds the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at index i
For each i, scan all earlier j where nums[j] < nums[i] and set len[i] = max(len[j] + 1)
Predecessor pointers recorded during the fill let you reconstruct the actual subsequence, not just the length
Every entry starts at 1 because any single element is an increasing subsequence of length 1
Time is O(n^2) and space is O(n); the n log n patience method is faster but harder to reconstruct from
Track the best overall length and its ending index to start the reconstruction

s1_definition.oneliner: Each cell is 1 + the best smaller-earlier cell, and predecessor links rebuild the actual run.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **LIS (Longest Increasing Subsequence)** – the longest subsequence of elements in strictly increasing order, not necessarily contiguous.
- **Tabulation** – fill an array where len[i] = length of LIS ending exactly at index i.
- **Recurrence** – for each i, scan all j < i where nums[j] < nums[i]; set len[i] = max(len[j] + 1).
- **Predecessor** – prev[i] records which j gave the best len[i], enabling reconstruction by walking backward.
- **Complexity** – O(n^2) time, O(n) space for the len and prev arrays.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants the longest run of strictly rising monthly balances in a customer's history, and needs to cite exactly which months formed that run for a credit report.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The quadratic tabulation for the Longest Increasing Subsequence is the version I reach for when I need the actual elements, not merely the length. I keep a length array where each entry holds the LIS length ending exactly at that index, starting every entry at 1. For each index, I scan all earlier indices, and whenever an earlier value is smaller and extending its run beats my current best, I update my length and record that earlier index as my predecessor.

The predecessor array makes reconstruction clean. After the fill, I know the best overall length and the ending index. I follow predecessor links backward, collecting each value, then reverse the list. The whole process is O(n^2) time and O(n) space.

The patience-sorting method gives O(n log n) time, which is faster for large inputs, but it only yields the length without extra bookkeeping. When the actual subsequence matters, the quadratic approach is simpler and more natural.

At the National Bank of India, a credit report needed to cite the exact months where Rajesh's balance strictly rose. I ran the quadratic fill over monthly balances and followed the predecessor chain to produce the list of improving months.

Remember one sentence: len[i] = 1 + the best len[j] where nums[j] < nums[i] and j < i, and prev[i] = j lets you walk backward to reconstruct the actual increasing subsequence.
